label: Revenge and Getting Even
framing: The wish to get even feels like justice from the inside, but it almost never restores what was taken and almost always costs the one who carries it. Scripture does not dismiss the wrong done to you, it takes it more seriously than you do, and then asks you to hand it to a Judge who will not get it wrong.
cultural: In the honor culture of the ancient world, a wrong unanswered was a shame that clung to a whole family, and blood feuds could run for generations. The law of an eye for an eye was itself a mercy, a limit set on a revenge that always wanted more, capping repayment at the size of the wound. Into that world Jesus went further still, calling his people to turn the cheek and to love the very enemy honor demanded they destroy.
historical: The early church astonished an empire built on retaliation by refusing to return harm, blessing those who cursed them and praying for those who killed them, following a Lord who had asked forgiveness for the men driving in the nails. Across the centuries, from the martyrs to the long Christian argument over just war and mercy, the church has held that vengeance belongs to God alone, and that the wronged are freed not by getting even but by laying the debt down.
application: Name the wrong honestly rather than minimizing it, since revenge often grows where a real injury was never acknowledged. Then do the harder, freer thing, hand the case to God who judges justly, instead of appointing yourself the one who collects. This is not the same as seeking lawful justice, which can be right and good, nor does it mean returning to harm. But the score you are determined to settle will rule you long after the one who wronged you has moved on.

verses.text: Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD.
verses.where: In the chapter that calls Israel to be holy as God is holy, the command not to seek revenge or bear a grudge stands in the same sentence as love your neighbor as yourself. The site's note calls that command the center of the chapter, grounded, like every command in it, in the refrain I am the LORD. Refusing revenge is not a New Testament novelty; it is part of the oldest law of love.

verses.text: Do not say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will repay the man according to his work.”
verses.where: Proverbs forbids the sentence that every wounded person has thought: I will do to him as he has done to me. The site's note says the sayings around it counsel fair judgment, honest words and refusing revenge, and warn against gloating when an enemy falls (Proverbs 24:17-18). Wisdom does not pretend the wrong was small; it refuses to let the wrong set the terms of your answer.

verses.text: May the LORD judge between you and me, and may the LORD take vengeance on you, but my hand will never be against you.
verses.where: David finds King Saul, who is hunting him, alone in a cave, and his men urge him to kill him; he cuts off a corner of Saul's robe and even that troubles his conscience. He calls out to Saul and asks the LORD to judge between them, but says his own hand will never be against him. The site's note says the chapter teaches restraint and trust in God's timing, not silence before injustice: David confronts Saul openly and flees rather than submitting to him.

verses.text: Blessed is your discernment, and blessed are you, because today you kept me from bloodshed and from avenging myself by my own hand.
verses.where: Insulted by Nabal, David sets out with four hundred men to wipe out his household, and Abigail meets him on the road and turns him back. David blesses her discernment for keeping him from bloodshed and from avenging himself by his own hand. The site's note says the chapter treats his grievance as real and his planned revenge as sin, and that his vow would have punished servants who had done nothing.

verses.text: But Joseph replied, “Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God?
verses.where: After their father's death, Joseph's brothers fear he will finally pay them back for selling him, and they bow before him. The site's note says his first words, am I in the place of God, refuse the role of judge their bowing offers him. The plain note adds that Joseph names what they did as evil, and that his words about God's purpose were said by the one wronged, years later, and are never a reason to explain away abuse.

verses.text: Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath. For it is written: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord.”
verses.where: Paul tells believers never to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath, quoting God's own claim that vengeance is his. The site's plain note says that blessing an enemy and leaving vengeance to God does not mean staying in danger or keeping silent about harm. Handing the score to God is not saying the score does not matter; it is trusting the only Judge who will settle it rightly.

verses.text: For he is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not carry the sword in vain. He is God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer.
verses.where: In the next breath Paul says the governing authority is God's servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer. The site's notes on Matthew 18 and 1 Corinthians 13 point to this verse when they say that crimes should be reported to the police and the proper authorities. Refusing personal revenge does not mean refusing justice; it means seeking it through the hands God has appointed for it.

verses.text: When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly.
verses.where: Peter says that when Christ was abused he did not retaliate, and when he suffered he made no threats, but entrusted himself to the one who judges justly. The site's note says the passage speaks to people with no way out about how to respond to mistreatment, and that it does not require anyone who can escape abuse to remain in it. Jesus' refusal of revenge was not the absence of justice but trust in the Judge.

verses.text: Then Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” And they divided up His garments by casting lots.
verses.where: Jesus' first word from the cross is a prayer for those who are crucifying him: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing. The site's note says prayer and indifference stand side by side in the verse, as the soldiers divide his clothes. The plain note says that ignorance does not make a wrong right, and that no one may use his death to justify hatred of anyone.

verses.text: Then men will say, “There is surely a reward for the righteous! There is surely a God who judges the earth!”
verses.where: This cursing psalm ends with people saying that there is surely a God who judges the earth. The site's note says the psalm is a prayer, not an action: the speaker gives his anger to God instead of taking revenge, and he speaks from the side of the victims of violent rulers. The plain note is firm that no reading of this psalm has ever made it right to harm anyone.

misread.taken: Eye for eye and tooth for tooth is often quoted as if the Bible gave people permission to get even, so that paying someone back in kind is simply justice.
misread.says: The site's note on the chapter says that in the law of Moses eye for eye was a principle for judges, limiting punishment to what fit the injury. It was given to courts to restrain revenge, not to individuals to license it. And Jesus, quoting it, goes further still: in your own cause, do not repay the evil person in kind.
misread.text: You have heard that it was said, ‘Eye for eye and tooth for tooth.’

misread.taken: Turn the other cheek is used to tell people who are being hurt that a Christian must take it, stay, and never seek protection.
misread.says: The site's plain note says plainly that turn the other cheek is not a command to stay with someone who is hurting you. Jesus speaks of refusing revenge, not of accepting abuse. When an officer struck him, Jesus asked why (John 18:23), and Paul used his rights under Roman law to stop a flogging (Acts 22:25). The note says seeking safety, and the protection of the law, is not disobedience to Jesus.
misread.text: But I tell you not to resist an evil person. If someone slaps you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also; if someone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well; and if someone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you.

whole: If you are thinking about hurting the person who hurt you, stop and talk to someone you trust today, a pastor, a counselor or a doctor; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. And if someone is still harming you, your safety comes first, and seeking protection is not revenge. The wish to get even can feel like justice from the inside. It replays the conversation and writes better answers. It imagines the other person's downfall, or plans a quieter payback: the truth told to the right people at the worst moment, the cold shoulder, the bad review, the story that will make them look as small as they made you feel. Sometimes it is fed by a wrong that was very great, and by the sense that no one else will ever hold them to account.

Scripture takes the wrong seriously; it does not tell the wounded that nothing happened. But it is honest about what revenge does. David, wronged by Nabal, set out to kill every male in his household, servants who had done nothing included, and was stopped only by Abigail on the road. Revenge almost always overshoots, because the one taking it is also the judge of his own case. It rarely restores what was taken. It binds the avenger to the person who hurt him, and it hands the wrong a second victory by shaping who he becomes. Most of us have wanted someone to pay, and most of us have also been, to someone, the one they wanted to make pay. That is part of why the Judge cannot be us.

So the Bible's wisdom is to refuse revenge without refusing justice. Do not repay evil for evil, Paul says, and leave room for God's wrath; Joseph, given every chance, asked whether he stood in the place of God. Take the anger to God in prayer, as the cursing psalms do, rather than acting it out. Where a crime was done, report it to the authorities God has appointed to punish wrongdoing; that is not revenge. Where you can, protect others from the one who harmed you. Let forgiveness do its slow work of letting go of the debt, which does not require trust, contact or silence. And watch for the small forms of payback, the gossip and the coldness, which are revenge wearing a smile.

The hope Scripture gives is that no wrong done to you is lost. There is surely a God who judges the earth, and he will not get it wrong. Christ, abused and crucified, did not retaliate but entrusted himself to that Judge, and prayed for those who killed him. On the cross God dealt with evil without becoming evil, and in the resurrection he showed that it would not have the last word. Handing the score to him is not weakness. It is the freedom of not having to carry it any longer.

differ.share: Christians agree that believers must never take personal revenge, that turn the other cheek is not a command to stay with someone who is hurting you, that seeking safety and the protection of the law is not disobedience to Jesus, and that crimes should be reported to the proper authorities.

views.name: No violence at all
views.body: Pacifists, such as the Anabaptists and their heirs the Mennonites, read do not resist an evil person as forbidding all violence.

views.name: Two kinds of duty
views.body: Martin Luther taught that in your own cause you should bear wrong without revenge, but that a ruler or judge must protect others and punish wrong (Romans 13:4).

views.name: Lawful force to protect the innocent
views.body: The just war tradition, from Augustine to Thomas Aquinas, holds that love of neighbor can require lawful force to protect the innocent, within strict limits.

differ.after: The site's notes on Matthew 5 set out these readings and do not decide between them. None of them permits personal revenge, and none asks a person being harmed to stay.

deep.sit: What would it mean for you to hand this wrong to the God who judges justly, and what are you afraid will happen if you do?

prayer.lead: A word to be still before the LORD and refrain from anger while wrongdoers seem to prosper. Pray it when the wish to get even will not let you rest.
prayer.text: Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him; do not fret when men prosper in their ways, when they carry out wicked schemes. Refrain from anger and abandon wrath; do not fret—it can only bring harm. For the evildoers will be cut off, but those who hope in the LORD will inherit the land.

careLines.text: Seeking safety, and the protection of the law, is not disobedience to Jesus.
If you are being harmed, tell someone you trust and get help.
One thing is not open: no reading of this psalm has ever made it right to harm anyone.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
